articles.title: The Socialist Labor Unionists Who Took On Samuel Gompers
articles.author: Philipp Corfman
articles.content_excerpt: “We have started on a great big national fight with the union movement at stake!” Max Hayes, socialist newspaper editor and union leader, thundered to the assembled representatives of Cleveland, Ohio’s labor movement in the fall of 1909. “The American Federation of Labor will stand or fall as events issue.” The delegates roared their approval, setting in motion a decisive battle for the soul of organized labor. On one side were Cleveland’s radical left-wing workers, led by Hayes; on the other, the AFL, led by archconservative President Samuel Gompers. articles.title: Swing Voters Want Kitchen-Table Populism, Not a Sermon
articles.author: Ned Rust
articles.content_excerpt: “Affordability” has now been embraced even by politicians who haven’t pushed a shopping cart since the Clinton administration. A record 89 percent of Americans say government corruption is widespread. And even mainstream liberal media is declaring that populism is dominating politics right now — so much so that Politico has an entire section devoted to the topic. But when it comes to winning swing voters, it’s not enough to speak like an elite-hating, anti-corruption populist whose number one priority is household costs. A key new study concludes that if you want to reach past your base, it will also behoove you to speak in concrete terms, to avoid sermonizing, and to steer clear of words you wouldn’t use in polite company. articles.title: We Rely on Cleaners’ Work, So Cleaners Should Be Paid More
articles.author: Hayat Elhore
articles.content_excerpt: Starting from the late 1970s, neoliberalism’s outsourcing revolution changed the lives of millions of low-wage service workers like cleaners. Once formerly employed by municipalities, national governments, or other public authorities to clean schools, hospitals, or airports, they now found themselves working for private companies contracted in competitive procurement markets. These workers have experienced job insecurity, rising workloads, draining shift work, and increasing isolation in the workplace. As procurement markets were designed to drive down prices, employers in labor-intensive sectors such as cleaning pressured fewer workers to deliver more. articles.title: When the Market Destroys a Community
articles.author: Evelina Johansson Wilén
articles.content_excerpt: In 1985, when I was four months old, my family moved from Kiruna to Luleå, a city in northern Sweden. My father had found a job with the Swedish State Railways, and we were given a firsthand rental contract for a four-room apartment in Hertsön, one of the city’s largest housing estates. Hertsön had been built as part of Sweden’s massive public housing program of the 1960s and ’70s. But there was another reason for its construction. It was meant to house workers for a vast new industrial project: Steelworks 80 (Stålverk 80). Steelworks 80 was conceived in the early 1970s by Sweden’s Social Democratic government as an expansion of the country’s steel industry. articles.content_excerpt: I was a freshman in high school in Alabama, I wore a hijab. In gym class my teacher wheeled in a screen. Something horrible was happening. I watched, mouth agape as the second tower hit. We were silent. Smoke pours from the World Trade Center after it was hit by two hijacked passenger planes September 11, 2001. I was sick to my stomach — had something happened to a family member? Did I know anyone in New York? Why was he there to pick me up? My father’s colleague did not answer me. Zeynab Muhammad, a Palestinian college student in Illinois in her early twenties, has been changing her routine since Israel began its assault on Gaza. She no longer goes to the library to study or roams campus to hang out with friends. She says it’s tough to complete schoolwork or get other tasks done. Fearing physical violence, she spends most of her time in her apartment. “ I’m constantly on edge,” she says about being on campus. ​ “ I feel like, when people look at me, all that comes to mind are the negative stereotypes associated with Arabs and Muslims. articles.title: The AfD's Economic Populism Could Hardly Be Shallower
articles.author: Alexander Görlach
articles.content_excerpt: It took less than an hour. No sooner had it become clear, this Sunday, that the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) was by far the strongest party in Saxony-Anhalt than Elon Musk offered his congratulations on X. The nationalist party’s lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, replied immediately, in English, offering “strong and constructive cooperation” and promising that, under AfD leadership, Germany would once again become “a place worth investing in.”This is the first time that a state chapter of the party, which the Office for the Protection of the Constitution classifies as “confirmed far-right extremist,” has actually won a state.
